subsystems.name: Rotor (mass stream)
subsystems.role: circulates inside the ring faster than orbital velocity; its outward centrifugal force is what holds everything up.
parts: magnetically levitated iron or ceramic pellets, or a segmented ribbon

subsystems.name: Sheath
subsystems.role: a non-rotating outer tube that sits still relative to the ground, carrying the station, motors and tethers.

subsystems.name: Levitation and drive
subsystems.role: keeps the rotor centred without touching the walls, and pumps energy back in to replace losses.

subsystems.name: Tethers
subsystems.role: cables hanging from the ring to ground anchors; these are the actual elevator shafts.

subsystems.name: Power and vacuum plant
subsystems.role: supplies the megawatts-to-gigawatts the drive needs and keeps the duct near-vacuum.
parts: solar arrays (or beamed power from the ground)

subsystems.name: Station and payload interface
subsystems.role: where cargo is transferred from tether climbers onto the ring and then launched or dropped to other orbits.

buildSteps.title: Choose the plane
buildSteps.detail: The ring is built over the equator, because a ring in any other plane would sweep across latitudes and its ground tethers could never stay fixed.

buildSteps.title: Learn to hold a loop up before building one
buildSteps.detail: Small uncrewed test loops — around the Moon, or a few-hundred-kilometre closed loop in low Earth orbit — prove that a circulating mass stream can be levitated, steered and kept from drifting into the walls.

buildSteps.title: Make the cable in space, not on Earth
buildSteps.detail: A ring roughly 40,000 km around is far too heavy to launch from the ground in one piece; it has to be manufactured from lunar or asteroid material and assembled by robots already in orbit.

buildSteps.title: Bootstrap the rotor
buildSteps.detail: Start with a thin, slow loop and spin it up gradually with linear motors. Well below orbital speed it has no support of its own and must be actively held, so control must work before the machine works.

buildSteps.title: Take the rotor past orbital speed
buildSteps.detail: As the rotor approaches about 8 km/s it begins to support itself; pushing it faster lets the same rotor carry an extra load, which is the stationary sheath.

buildSteps.title: Extend and levitate the sheath
buildSteps.detail: Segment by segment, the outer tube is threaded around the rotor and held up by it. Because the sheath does not rotate, it carries no hoop stress — only its own weight between supports.

buildSteps.title: Add drive stations and power
buildSteps.detail: Linear motors spaced along the ring top up the rotor's energy against drag, eddy-current and pumping losses; solar arrays or ground-beamed power feed them.

buildSteps.title: Lower the tethers
buildSteps.detail: Cables are paid down from the ring to anchored ground stations. Vehicles climb them, carrying payload from the surface to the ring.

buildSteps.title: Commission and operate
buildSteps.detail: The ring is brought up to full speed, debris and satellite avoidance is automated, and rotor segments are replaced on a rolling maintenance schedule that must never stop.

prerequisites.why: maglev trains, flywheels and particle-accelerator magnets exist, but nothing has run a 8–15 km/s rotor in vacuum for years at a time.
a 40,000 km structure can only be built by robots from space-sourced material, and that industry is in its infancy.
reusable rockets have cut prices sharply, but building the first bootstrap loop still needs hundreds of heavy launches.

prerequisites.tech: Vacuum and cryogenic engineering at kilometre scale
prerequisites.why: the duct must stay near-vacuum over enormous distances; leaks and outgassing are cumulative problems.
megawatt solar arrays work today, but the drive losses of a full ring are far larger.
a ring at low altitude crosses the paths of thousands of tracked objects and must be steered around them.

pathway.milestone: paper designs and small demonstrators of active-support structures (launch loops, space elevators and ring concepts) alongside today's maglev, vacuum-tube and tether experiments
pathway.unlocks: proof that a circulating mass stream can be levitated and controlled at all.

pathway.milestone: an uncrewed ring around an airless body such as the Moon, where low gravity and no atmosphere make a small ring far easier
pathway.unlocks: experience in building, spinning up and maintaining a closed loop in space.

pathway.milestone: a partial Earth ring or launch-loop precursor that throws payloads to orbit without a rocket
pathway.unlocks: cheap bulk transport, which is the only thing that makes a full ring affordable.

pathway.milestone: a complete equatorial ring with ground tethers and a station
pathway.unlocks: routine surface-to-orbit access at any hour, plus a platform for assembling and launching deep-space vehicles.

pathway.milestone: additional rings at other inclinations and latitudes, linked into a planet-wide transport and power grid
pathway.unlocks: a civilisational-scale logistics system whose economics are still unproven.
